claim: Lattices provide solutions for optimal packings, efficient resource distribution, and cryptographic protocols.
source: These arrangements provide solutions for optimal packings, efficient resource distribution, and cryptographic protocols.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about lattices in the abstract without specific experimental data from this manuscript.

claim: For mammals navigating on a surface, hexagonal activity patterns of grid cells are optimal.
source: For mammals navigating on a surface, we show that the hexagonal activity patterns of grid cells are optimal.
evidence: This is the main theoretical result derived in the manuscript using Fisher information analysis.

claim: For species that move freely in three dimensions, a face-centered cubic lattice is best for grid cell activity patterns.
source: For species that move freely in three dimensions, a face-centered cubic lattice is best.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the mathematical analysis of optimal lattices in 3D.

claim: The prediction about face-centered cubic lattices could be tested experimentally in flying bats, arboreal monkeys, or marine mammals.
source: This prediction could be tested experimentally in flying bats, arboreal monkeys, or marine mammals.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future experimental tests.

claim: The brain encodes higher-dimensional sensory or cognitive variables with populations of grid-cell-like neurons whose activity patterns exhibit lattice structures at multiple, nested scales.
source: More generally, our theory suggests that the brain encodes higher-dimensional sensory or cognitive variables with populations of grid-cell-like neurons whose activity patterns exhibit lattice structures at multiple, nested scales.
evidence: This is a theoretical hypothesis based on the mathematical results presented.

claim: Place cells discharge when an animal is near one particular location in its environment.
source: 'Place cells' discharge when an animal is near one particular location in its environment (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Grid cells are active at multiple locations that span an imaginary hexagonal lattice covering the environment.
source: 'Grid cells' are active at multiple locations that span an imaginary hexagonal lattice covering the environment (Hafting et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Grid cells have been found in rats, mice, crawling bats, and human beings.
source: and have been found in rats, mice, crawling bats, and human beings (Hafting et al., 2005; Fyhn et al., 2008; Yartsev et al., 2011; Jacobs et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Grid cells are believed to build a metric for space.
source: These cells are believed to build a metric for space.
evidence: This is stated as a general belief in the field without specific citation.

claim: Theoretical and numerical studies suggest that the hexagonal lattice structure is best suited for representing two-dimensional space.
source: Theoretical and numerical studies suggest that the hexagonal lattice structure is best suited for representing such a two-dimensional (2D) space (Guanella and Verschure, 2007; Mathis, 2012; Wei et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical and numerical work.

claim: The neuronal representation of 3D space in animals may consist of a mosaic of lower-dimensional patches.
source: Their neuronal representation of 3D space may consist of a mosaic of lower-dimensional patches (Jeffery et al., 2013), as evidenced by recordings from climbing rats (Hayman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Place cells in flying bats represent 3D space in a uniform and nearly isotropic manner.
source: Place cells in flying bats, on the other hand, represent 3D space in a uniform and nearly isotropic manner (Yartsev and Ulanovsky, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: The resolution of a grid module can be mapped onto the problem of packing non-overlapping spheres.
source: we show how resolving the population's FI can be mapped onto the problem of packing non-overlapping spheres, which also plays an important role in other coding problems and cryptography (Shannon, 1948; Conway and Sloane, 1992; Gray and Neuhoff, 1998).
evidence: This is a theoretical result derived in the manuscript, with citations to related work in other fields.

claim: The optimal lattices are the ones with the highest packing ratio—the densest lattices represent space most accurately.
source: The optimal lattices are thus the ones with the highest packing ratio—the densest lattices represent space most accurately.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion derived from the mathematical analysis in the manuscript.

claim: Hexagonal lattices are optimal for representing 2D space.
source: This remarkably simple and straightforward answer implies that hexagonal lattices are optimal for representing 2D space.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion derived from the mathematical analysis.

claim: In 3D, grid cells will have firing fields positioned on a face-centered-cubic lattice or its equally dense non-lattice variant—a hexagonal close packing structure.
source: In 3D, our theory makes the experimentally testable prediction that grid cells will have firing fields positioned on a face-centered-cubic lattice or its equally dense non-lattice variant—a hexagonal close packing structure.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the mathematical analysis.

claim: Unimodal tuning curves with a single preferred stimulus have been extensively studied.
source: Unimodal tuning curves with a single preferred stimulus, which are characteristic for place cells or orientation-selective neurons in visual cortex, have been extensively studied (Paradiso, 1988; Seung and Sompolinsky, 1993; Pouget et al., 1999; Zhang and Sejnowski, 1999; Bethge et al., 2002; Eurich and Wilke, 2000; Brown and Bäcker, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Multimodal tuning curves that are periodic along orthogonal stimulus axes and generate repeating hypercubic activation patterns have been studied.
source: This is also true for multimodal tuning curves that are periodic along orthogonal stimulus axes and generate repeating hypercubic (or hyper-rectangular) activation patterns (Montemurro and Panzeri, 2006; Fiete et al., 2008; Mathis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Optimal lattices will be found in the representation of other high-dimensional sensory or cognitive spaces.
source: Our results extend these studies by taking more general stimulus symmetries into account and lead us to hypothesize that optimal lattices not only underlie the neural representation of physical space, but will also be found in the representation of other high-dimensional sensory or cognitive spaces.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the theoretical results.

claim: The trial-to-trial variability of any two neurons is assumed to be independent of each other in the population coding model.
source: While two neurons can have correlated tuning curves Ωi(x), we assume that the trial-to-trial variability of any two neurons is independent of each other.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption of the model.

claim: The inverse of the Fisher information matrix bounds the covariance matrix of the estimated coordinates.
source: bounds the covariance matrix ∑(x^|x) of the estimated coordinates x = (x1,…,xD)
evidence: This is a mathematical result known as the Cramér-Rao bound.

claim: The Cramér-Rao bound states that the resolution of any unbiased estimator cannot be greater than the inverse of the Fisher information.
source: The resolution of any unbiased estimator of the encoded stimulus can achieve cannot be greater than J(x)−1. This is known as the Cramér-Rao bound (Lehmann, 1998).
evidence: This is a well-known result from statistical theory, supported by citation.

claim: Isotropy does not entail that the global spatial tuning of an individual neuron has to be radially symmetric, but merely that the errors are locally distributed according to a radially symmetric distribution.
source: Isotropy does not entail that the (global) spatial tuning of an individual neuron, Ωi(x), has to be radially symmetric, but merely that the errors are (locally) distributed according to a radially symmetric distribution.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mathematical concept of isotropy in the context of the model.

claim: The tuning curve of a grid cell with hexagonal tuning is not radially symmetric around the center of a field, but the posterior is radially symmetric around any given location for a module of such grid cells.
source: For instance, the tuning curve of a grid cell with hexagonal tuning is not radially symmetric around the center of a field (it has three axes), but the posterior is radially symmetric around any given location for a module of such grid cells.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of grid cell modules.

claim: Homogeneity requires that the Fisher information be asymptotically independent of position as the number of neurons becomes large.
source: Homogeneity requires that the FI J(x) be asymptotically independent of x (as the number of neurons N becomes large)
evidence: This is a definition of homogeneity in the context of the model.

claim: Spatial isotropy implies that all diagonal entries in the Fisher information matrix are equal.
source: spatial isotropy implies that all diagonal entries in the FI matrix J(x) are equal.
evidence: This is a mathematical consequence of the definition of isotropy.

claim: The Fisher information of the rescaled module is λ−2 times the Fisher information of the original module.
source: Indeed, as we show in the 'Material and methods' section, the FI of the rescaled module is λ−2 Jς(0).
evidence: This is a mathematical result derived in the manuscript.

claim: The local resolution of an unbiased estimator could rapidly improve with a finer grid size.
source: The Cramér-Rao bound (Equation 4) implies that the local resolution of an unbiased estimator could thus rapidly improve with a finer grid size, that is, decreasing λ.
evidence: This is an inference from the Cramér-Rao bound and the scaling properties.

claim: For any grid module, the posterior probability is periodic.
source: However, for any grid module ς=(Ω,ρ,L) the posterior probability, that is, the likelihood of possible positions given a particular spike count vector K = (k1,…,kN), is also periodic.
evidence: This is derived from Bayes rule and the periodic structure of grid cells.

claim: The multiple firing fields of a grid cell cannot be distinguished by a decoder.
source: Thus, the multiple firing fields of a grid cell cannot be distinguished by a decoder, so that for λ → 0 the global resolution approaches the a priori uncertainty (Mathis et al., 2012a, 2012b).
evidence: This is an inference from the periodicity of the posterior, supported by citations.

claim: By combining multiple grid modules with different spatial periods one can overcome the fundamental limitation caused by periodicity.
source: By combining multiple grid modules with different spatial periods one can overcome this fundamental limitation, counteracting the ambiguity caused by periodicity and still preserving the highest resolution at the smallest scale.
evidence: This is an inference about how nested grid modules can resolve ambiguity.

claim: The Fisher information for an individual module at one scale determines the optimal length scale of the next module.
source: The FI for an individual module at one scale determines the optimal length scale of the next module (Mathis et al., 2012a, 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The larger the Fisher information per module, the greater the refinement at subsequent scales can be.
source: The larger the FI per module, the greater the refinement at subsequent scales can be (Mathis et al., 2012a, 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The resolution of the grid module is inversely proportional to the volumes of their fundamental domains.
source: which signifies that the resolution of the grid module is inversely proportional to the volumes of their fundamental domains.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mathematical result.

claim: The periodic structure has a direct impact on the resolution of the grid module.
source: The periodic structure L thus has a direct impact on the resolution of the grid module.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical analysis.

claim: Finding the maximum Fisher information translates directly into finding the lattice with the highest packing ratio.
source: This result implies that finding the maximum FI translates directly into finding the lattice with the highest packing ratio.
evidence: This is a key theoretical conclusion of the manuscript.

claim: The sphere packing problem has wide-ranging applications from crystallography to information theory.
source: The sphere packing problem is of general interest in mathematics (Conway and Sloane, 1992) and has wide-ranging applications from crystallography to information theory (Barlow, 1883; Shannon, 1948; Whittaker, 1981; Gray and Neuhoff, 1998; Gruber, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Among grid modules with different lattices, the lattice with the highest packing ratio leads to the highest spatial resolution.
source: We now come to the main finding of this study: among grid modules with different lattices, the lattice with the highest packing ratio leads to the highest spatial resolution.
evidence: This is the main theoretical result of the manuscript.

claim: The condition that the support of the tuning shape is contained within the fundamental domain is consistent with experimental observations that grid cells tend to stop firing between grid fields.
source: The condition supp(Ω) = [0, R] with BR(0) ⊂ L, although restrictive, is consistent with experimental observations that grid cells tend to stop firing between grid fields and that the typical ratio between field radius and spatial period is well below 1/2 (Hafting et al., 2005; Brun et al., 2008; Giocomo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: The optimal tuning width for Gaussian tuning curves increases with the number of spatial dimensions.
source: The same observation will hold in higher dimensions (D > 2), consistent with the finding that the optimal tuning width for Gaussian tuning curves increases with the number of spatial dimensions, whether space is infinite (Zhang and Sejnowski, 1999) or finite (Brown and Bäcker, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: When the radius of the support of the tuning curve exceeds the in-radius, the optimal lattice can be different from the densest one.
source: When the radius R of the support of the tuning curve exceeds the in-radius, the optimal lattice can be different from the densest one as we will show numerically for specific tuning curves and Poisson noise.
evidence: This is demonstrated numerically in the manuscript.

claim: With well separated fields, the densest lattice provides the highest resolution for any tuning shape.
source: However, with well separated fields, like those observed experimentally, the densest lattice provides the highest resolution for any tuning shape Ω, as we just demonstrated.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion from the mathematical analysis.

claim: The hexagonal lattice is the optimal arrangement for grid-cell firing fields on the plane.
source: According to Equation 14, the hexagonal lattice is the optimal arrangement for grid-cell firing fields on the plane.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical analysis.

claim: The hexagonal lattice outperforms the quadratic lattice by about 15.5%.
source: For example, it outperforms the quadratic lattice, which has a density of π/4, by about 15.5% (see Figure 2).
evidence: This is calculated from the packing ratios and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The Fisher information of a grid module periodified along a hexagonal lattice outperforms one periodified along a square lattice by about 15.5%.
source: Consequently, the FI of a grid module periodified along a hexagonal lattice outperforms one periodified along a square lattice by the same factor.
evidence: This follows from the relationship between packing ratio and Fisher information.

claim: As the support radius becomes larger than 1/2, the Fisher information of the hexagonal lattice is no longer necessarily greater than that of the square lattice.
source: As the support radius becomes larger, the FI of the hexagonal lattice is no longer necessarily greater than that of the square lattice; the specific interplay of tuning curve and boundary shape determines which lattice is better
evidence: This is observed in the numerical results.

claim: The Fisher information falls like 1/sin(φ) so that the maximum is achieved for the hexagonal lattice with π/3.
source: Indeed, according to Equation 13, the FI falls like 1/det L=1/sin(φ) so that the maximum is achieved for the hexagonal lattice with π/3.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical relationship and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Because of fluctuations in the Fisher information, the square lattice is better than the hexagonal lattice in about 20% of cases for populations of 200 neurons.
source: Because of fluctuations in the FI, however, the square lattice is better than the hexagonal lattice in about 20% of the cases.
evidence: This is observed in the numerical simulations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: For radially symmetric tuning curves the hexagonal lattice provides the best resolution among all planar lattices.
source: Our theory implies that for radially symmetric tuning curves the hexagonal lattice provides the best resolution among all planar lattices.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the theoretical analysis.

claim: Wei et al. demonstrated that a population of nested grid cells with hexagonal tuning is optimal for winner-take-all and Bayesian maximum likelihood decoders.
source: Wei et al. considered a notion of resolution defined as the range of the population code per smallest distinguishable scale and then demonstrated that a population of nested grid cells with hexagonal tuning is optimal for a winner-take-all and Bayesian maximum likelihood decoders (Wei et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Guanella and Verschure numerically compared hexagonal to other regular lattices based on maximum likelihood decoding.
source: Guanella and Verschure numerically compared hexagonal to other regular lattices based on maximum likelihood decoding (Guanella and Verschure, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The optimal 3D grid-cell tuning is given by the face-centered cubic lattice.
source: This implies that the optimal 3D grid-cell tuning is given by the FCC lattice.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical result about packing ratios.

claim: As long as the support θ2 of the tuning shape is smaller than 1/2, the trace of the population Fisher information of the face-centered cubic lattice outperforms both the body-centered cubic and cubic lattices.
source: As long as the support θ2 of Ω is smaller than 1/2, the support is a subset of the fundamental domain of all three lattices. Hence, the trace of the population FI of the FCC outperforms both the BCC and C lattices.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and follows from the theory.

claim: Face-centered cubic grid cells provide roughly 41% more resolution for the same number of neurons than cubic grid cells.
source: As the ratios of the trace of the population FI scales with the packing ratio (Figure 4C), FCC-grid cells provide roughly 41% more resolution for the same number of neurons than do C-grid cells.
evidence: This is calculated from the packing ratios and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Face-centered cubic grid cells provide 8.8% more Fisher information than body-centered cubic grid cells.
source: Similarly, FCC-grid cells provide 8.8% more FI than BCC-grid cells.
evidence: This is calculated from the packing ratios.

claim: Despite the small module size of 200 neurons, face-centered cubic lattice outperformed the cubic lattice in all simulated realizations.
source: Despite the small module size, FCC outperformed the cubic lattice C in all simulated realizations.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E through numerical simulations.

claim: The face-centered cubic lattice is generated by stacking hexagonal layers in a specific sequence.
source: This stacking of layers is shown in Figure 5C and generates the FCC lattice.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 5C.

claim: Hexagonal close packing is as tightly packed as the face-centered cubic lattice but cannot be described by three vectors and thus does not define a lattice.
source: Yet as this arrangement, called hexagonal close packing (HCP), cannot be described by three vectors, it does not define a lattice (see Figure 5D), even though it is as tightly packed as the FCC.
evidence: This is explained in the text and illustrated in Figure 5D.

claim: Grid modules comprising face-centered cubic or hexagonal close packing symmetries have the same Fisher information.
source: we can conclude that grid modules comprising FCC or HCP-like symmetries have the same FI.
evidence: This is derived mathematically in the manuscript.

claim: For bump-like tuning curves, the Fisher information of hexagonal close packing and face-centered cubic lattice modules are identical.
source: For bump-like tuning curves Ω, both FIs are identical (Figure 5E) as expected from the radial symmetry of Ω.
evidence: This is shown numerically in Figure 5E.

claim: Grid cells defined by either hexagonal close packing or face-centered cubic symmetries provide optimal resolution.
source: As a consequence, grid cells defined by either HCP or FCC symmetries provide optimal resolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical and numerical analysis.

claim: All optimal packings in 3D share one feature: around each sphere there are exactly 12 spheres, arranged in either hexagonal close packing or face-centered cubic lattice fashion.
source: All packings share one feature: around each sphere there are exactly 12 spheres, arranged in either HCP or FCC lattice fashion (Hales, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to mathematical work.

claim: It has been proven that no other arrangement has a higher packing ratio than the face-centered cubic lattice.
source: Only in recent years has it been proven that no other arrangement has a higher packing ratio than the FCC, a problem known as Kepler's conjecture (Hales, 2005, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mathematical proofs.

claim: While there are equally dense packings as the densest lattice in 3D, this is not the case in 2D.
source: While there are equally dense packings as the densest lattice in 3D, this is not the case in 2D.
evidence: This is stated based on mathematical knowledge.

claim: Thue proved that the hexagonal lattice is unique in being the densest amongst all planar packings.
source: Thue proved that the hexagonal lattice is unique in being the densest amongst all planar packings (Thue, 1910)
evidence: This is a well-known mathematical result, supported by citation.

claim: Grid cells in 2D should possess a hexagonal lattice structure.
source: grid cells in 2D should possess a hexagonal lattice structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical analysis.

claim: The resolution of a grid module is related to the packing ratio of the lattice.
source: We find that the resolution of a grid module is related to the packing ratio of L—the lattice with highest packing ratio corresponds to the grid module with highest resolution.
evidence: This is the main theoretical finding of the manuscript.

claim: A common feature of optimal solutions in 3D is that each grid field is surrounded by 12 other grid fields, arranged in either face-centered cubic lattice or hexagonal close packing fashion.
source: A common feature of these highly symmetric optimal solutions in 3D is that each grid field is surrounded by 12 other grid fields, arranged in either FCC lattice or hexagonal close packing fashion.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical analysis of optimal packings.

claim: Resolution alone, as measured by the Fisher information, does not distinguish between optimal packing solutions with different symmetries.
source: However, resolution alone, as measured by the FI, does not distinguish between optimal packing solutions with different symmetries.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis showing equal Fisher information for different optimal packings.

claim: Using the Fisher information makes finding the optimal lattice analytically tractable for all dimensions.
source: As we have demonstrated, using the FI makes finding the optimal L analytically tractable for all dimensions D and singles out densest lattices as optimal tuning shapes under assumptions that are restrictive, but are consistent with experimental measurements (Hafting et al., 2005; Brun et al., 2008; Giocomo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a summary of the methodological contribution, with citations to experimental support.

claim: Numerical simulations showed that for broader tuning curves, grid modules with quadratic lattices can provide more Fisher information than the hexagonal lattice.
source: Indeed, our numerical simulations also showed that for broader tuning curves, grid modules with quadratic lattices can provide more FI than the hexagonal lattice (Figure 3A, θ2 ≈ 0.6 and θ1 = 1/4)
evidence: This is shown in the numerical results in Figure 3A.

claim: Grid cells with cubic or body-centered cubic lattice can provide more Fisher information than face-centered cubic lattice for certain tuning parameters.
source: and that grid cells with a C or BCC lattice can provide more FI than the FCC (Figure 4B, θ2 > 0.65 and θ1 = 1/4).
evidence: This is shown in the numerical results in Figure 4B.

claim: Guanella and Verschure showed numerically that triangular tessellations yield lower reconstruction errors under maximum-likelihood decoding than equivalently scaled square grids.
source: For the planar case, Guanella and Verschure (2007) show numerically that triangular tessellations yield lower reconstruction errors under maximum-likelihood decoding than equivalently scaled square grids.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Wei et al. provide a mathematical argument that hexagonal grids are optimal.
source: Complementing this numerical analysis, Wei et al. (2013) provide a mathematical argument that hexagonal grids are optimal.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: For asymptotically efficient decoders like maximum likelihood or minimum mean square estimator, the resolution can attain the bound given by the Fisher information for large neuron numbers and expected peak spike counts.
source: For large neuron numbers N and expected peak spike counts fmaxτ the resolution of asymptotically efficient decoders, like the maximum likelihood decoder, or the minimum mean square estimator, can indeed attain the resolution bound given by the FI (Seung and Sompolinsky, 1993; Bethge et al., 2002; Mathis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: For small neuron numbers and peak spike counts, the optimal codes could be different from those predicted by Fisher information.
source: In contrast, for small neuron numbers and peak spike counts, the optimal codes could be different, just as it has been shown in the past that the optimal tuning width in these cases cannot be predicted by the FI (Bethge et al., 2002; Yaeli et al., 2010; Berens et al., 2011; Mathis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Optimal populations with hexagonal patterns provide 15.5% more resolution than grid codes with quadratic grid cells for the same number of neurons in 2D.
source: Quantitatively, we demonstrated that these optimal populations provide 15.5% (2D) and about 41% (3D) more resolution than grid codes with quadratic or cubic grid cells for the same number of neurons.
evidence: This is calculated from the packing ratios.

claim: Optimal populations with face-centered cubic patterns provide about 41% more resolution than grid codes with cubic grid cells for the same number of neurons in 3D.
source: Quantitatively, we demonstrated that these optimal populations provide 15.5% (2D) and about 41% (3D) more resolution than grid codes with quadratic or cubic grid cells for the same number of neurons.
evidence: This is calculated from the packing ratios.

claim: Medial entorhinal cortex harbors a nested grid code with at least 5 and potentially 10 or more modules.
source: However, as medial entorhinal cortex harbors a nested grid code with at least 5 and potentially 10 or more modules (Stensola et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Aligned grid-cell lattices with perfectly periodic tuning curves imply that the posterior is periodic.
source: Because aligned grid-cell lattices with perfectly periodic tuning curves imply that the posterior is periodic too (compare Equation 8)
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical analysis.

claim: Information from different scales would have to be combined to yield an unambiguous read-out.
source: information from different scales would have to be combined to yield an unambiguous read-out.
evidence: This is an inference about how nested grid codes could be decoded.

claim: The slight but apparently persistent irregularities in the firing fields across space might be used for decoding.
source: An alternative hypothesis, as first suggested by Hafting et al., is that the slight, but apparently persistent irregularities in the firing fields across space (Hafting et al., 2005; Krupic et al., 2015; Stensola et al., 2015) are being used.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: The first recordings of grid cells showed that the fields are not exactly hexagonally arranged and that different fields might have different peak firing rates.
source: However, the first recordings of grid cells already showed that the fields are not exactly hexagonally arranged and that different fields might have different peak firing rates (Hafting et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental observations.

claim: Deviations from hexagonal symmetry have gained considerable attention recently.
source: More recently, deviations from hexagonal symmetry have gained considerable attention (Derdikman et al., 2009; Krupic et al., 2013, 2015; Stensola et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent experimental work.

claim: Defects in grid cell periodicity might imply that a decoder might be able to distinguish different unit cells even given a single module.
source: Such 'defects' modulate the periodicity of the tuning and consequently affect the symmetry of the likelihood function. This might imply that a potential decoder might be able to distinguish different unit cells even given a single module, which is not possible for perfectly periodic tuning curves (compare Equation 8).
evidence: This is an inference about the potential consequences of irregularities.

claim: The local resolution is robust to small, incoherent variations in grid cell tuning.
source: The local resolution, on the other hand, is robust to small, incoherent variations as the FI is a statistical average over many tuning curves with different spatial phases.
evidence: This is an inference from the mathematical properties of Fisher information.

claim: Small variations in the peak rate and grid fields will average out unless these variations are coherent across grid cells.
source: Small variations in the peak rate and grid fields will therefore average out, unless these variations are coherent across grid cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the averaging properties of Fisher information.

claim: Resolution bounded by the Fisher information is robust with respect to minor differences in peak firing rates and hexagonality.
source: Thus, resolution bounded by the FI is robust with respect to minor differences in peak firing rates and hexagonality.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of variations.

claim: The topology of natural habitats can be highly complicated.
source: Indeed, the topology of natural habitats, such as burrows or caves, can be highly complicated.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge.

claim: Higher resolution might be required at spatial locations of behavioral relevance.
source: Higher resolution might be required at spatial locations of behavioral relevance.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential requirements for spatial coding.

claim: Neural representations of 3D space may be composed of multiple 1D and 2D patches.
source: Neural representations of 3D space may also be composed of multiple 1D and 2D patches (Jeffery et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: An isotropic and homogeneous representation for space can emerge out of non-Euclidean perceptual spaces by learning the motion group.
source: Poincaré already suggested that an isotropic and homogeneous representation for space can emerge out of non-Euclidean perceptual spaces, as one can move through physical space by learning the motion group (Poincaré, 1913).
evidence: This is supported by citation to historical theoretical work.

claim: An isotropic and homogeneous representation of 3D space facilitates mental rotations in 3D and yields local coordinates that are independent of the environment's topology.
source: An isotropic and homogeneous representation of 3D space facilitates (mental) rotations in 3D and yields local coordinates that are independent of the environment's topology.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional advantages of isotropic representations.

claim: The efficient-coding hypothesis would argue that surface-bound animals might not need to dedicate their limited neuronal resources to acquiring a full representation of space.
source: On the other hand, the efficient-coding hypothesis (Barlow, 1959; Atick, 1992; Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001) would argue that surface-bound animals might not need to dedicate their limited neuronal resources to acquiring a full representation of space, as flying animals might have to do
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Representations of 3D space will be species-specific.
source: so that representations of 3D space will be species-specific (Las and Ulanovsky, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Desert ants represent space only as a projection to flat space.
source: Desert ants represent space only as a projection to flat space (Wohlgemuth et al., 2001; Grah et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Experimental evidence suggests that rats do not encode 3D space in an isotropic manner.
source: Likewise, experimental evidence suggests that rats do not encode 3D space in an isotropic manner (Hayman et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: The anisotropic spatial representation in rats might be a consequence of the specific anisotropic spatial navigation tasks these rats had to perform.
source: but this might be a consequence of the specific anisotropic spatial navigation tasks these rats had to perform.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of observed anisotropy.

claim: The 3D, toroidal head-direction system in bats suggests that they have access to the full motion group.
source: The 3D, toroidal head-direction system in bats also suggests that they have access to the full motion group (Finkelstein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Face-centered cubic and hexagonal close packing solutions evolve dynamically in a self-organizing network model for 3D.
source: Interestingly, such solutions also evolve dynamically in a self-organizing network model for 3D (Stella et al., 2013; Stella and Treves, 2015) that extends a previous 2D system which exhibits hexagonal grid patterns (Kropff and Treves, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to computational modeling work.

claim: Walls can intersect the firing fields of grid cells.
source: In particular, the firing fields are not required to be contained within the confines of the four walls of a box—experimental observations show that walls can intersect the firing fields (so that one measures only a part of the firing field).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: The borders clearly distort the hexagonal arrangement of nearby firing fields in 2D environments.
source: On the other hand, the borders clearly distort the hexagonal arrangement of nearby firing fields in 2D environments (Stensola et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Central firing fields are more perfectly arranged than those near borders.
